title: A covenant (CCC 1601; 1644)
hookLine: marriage as a lifelong covenant of partners

cards: A phone contract has a term. A lease has an end date. A gym membership lasts until you find the cancel button.
Contracts are useful: they say what each side owes, for how long, and what happens if someone doesn't deliver.
Then, on a Saturday afternoon, two people stand at the front of a church and promise something with no end date and no exit clause: for better, for worse, in sickness and in health.
Whatever that is, it's not a phone plan.

teach.h: A PARTNERSHIP OF THE WHOLE OF LIFE.
teach.b: The Catechism opens its teaching on marriage with this word: covenant.
Marriage, it says, is a covenant by which a man and a woman form a partnership of the whole of life, ordered to the good of the spouses and to the procreation and education of children.
Between the baptized, Christ raised it to the dignity of a sacrament. What makes a covenant different? Some teachers put it this way.

teach.h: A CONTRACT TRADES THINGS. A COVENANT GIVES PERSONS.
teach.b: A contract trades things: money for a service, rent for a room. A covenant gives persons. A contract says, I'll do this if you do that.
A covenant says, I am yours.

Covenants run through the Bible: God makes them with Noah, with Abraham, with Israel at Sinai, and the prophets reach for marriage to describe them, God as a faithful husband who doesn't walk away, even when his people do.
So calling marriage a covenant borrows the language of God's own faithfulness.
Genesis, in the Douay-Rheims: "Wherefore a man shall leave father and mother, and shall cleave to his wife: and they shall be two in one flesh."

The love of the spouses, the Catechism says, by its nature asks for unity and indissolubility, a partnership for the whole of life, and for faithfulness, rooted in God's own fidelity and Christ's love for the Church.
That's why a Catholic wedding has vows, not terms. The couple give consent freely, before witnesses.
And in the Latin Church, Catholic teaching says the couple are themselves the ministers of the sacrament: the priest or deacon witnesses, and the two give it to each other.

how: At a Catholic wedding the bride and groom freely exchange their consent and vows before a priest or deacon and witnesses, and the Church regards the couple themselves as the ministers of the sacrament.

o: a legal deal that sets each side's duties
an engagement promise made before a wedding
a lifelong gift of persons, sealed by vows

practice: Bring to mind one couple who are struggling right now, whether you know the details or only the silence at dinner. Don't take sides or try to fix it; just hold the two of them together in your mind, side by side.
If you pray, ask God to strengthen what they promised each other; if you don't, wish them patience and honest words.

wordCard.voice: A covenant. Not a trade of things, but a gift of persons: in Catholic teaching, marriage is a partnership of the whole of life, faithful and for life, raised by Christ to a sacrament. Today's word.

orig.note: Hebrew: covenant, the word for God's covenants in the Hebrew Bible.
